The Bhagavad Gita. A 700-verse philosophical dialogue embedded within the epic Mahabharata, composed around the second century BCE. It contains the god Krishna counseling the warrior Arjuna on duty, righteousness, and spiritual liberation, and it stands as Hinduism's most widely read scripture.

The dialogue is set on a battlefield at Kurukshetra, where Arjuna faces moral crisis before fighting his cousins. Krishna serves as his charioteer and spiritual guide, composed in Sanskrit as 18 chapters within the much larger Mahabharata epic, traditionally authored by Vyasa.

The Gita teaches three primary paths to liberation, called moksha: karma yoga, action without attachment; bhakti yoga, devotion; and jnana yoga, knowledge. One of the most iconic moments comes in Chapter 11, when Krishna reveals his divine form, the Vishvarupa. This revelation is central to bhakti devotional movements and has influenced Advaita Vedanta non-dualism, Tantra, and modern Hindu philosophy.

A central teaching captures the Gita's practical wisdom: you have a right to perform your prescribed duty, but you are not entitled to the fruits of action. This karma yoga principle extends Hindu philosophy beyond the Vedas and Upanishads, making it accessible to all castes and classes. The dialogue itself is driven forward by Arjuna's crisis and questioning, while Krishna imparts the wisdom. The Mahabharata as a whole forms the epic context from which this Gita emerges, building upon and interpreting Vedic knowledge for human practice.
